attributes (data members), methods (functions), aur unke relationships (jaise inheritance, association) ko dikhata hai. Ye software design ke planning phase mein use hota hai.\n-\n🔷 Example (Real-life Analogy):\nSocho tum ek hospital management system bana rahe ho.\nTumhare paas ek Doctor class hogi, jisme doctor ka name, specialization, aur methods jaise diagnosePatient() honge.\u000b\nEk Patient class hogi, jisme name, age, aur admit() jaisa method hoga.\u000b\nDono classes ke beech relation bhi ho sakta hai — jaise \"Doctor treats Patient\".\u000b\n-\n🔷 Class Diagram Ka Structure:\n1. Class Box:\nEk class ko 3 parts mein divide kiya jaata hai:\nlua\nCopyEdit\n------------------------\n|       ClassName        |\n|------------------------|\n|  + attribute1: type    |\n|  - attribute2: type    |\n|------------------------|\n|  + method1(): return   |\n|  - method2(): return   |\n ------------------------\n\n+ → public\u000b\n- → private\u000b\n# → protected\u000b\n2. Attributes:\nClass ke variables ya data members hote hain. Example:\u000b +name: String, -age: int\n3. Methods (Operations):\nClass ke functions hote hain. Example:\u000b +getName(): String, -calculateAge(): int\n-\n🔷 Relationships in Class Diagram:\n\u0010\u0012\u001cRelationship Type\n\u001cSymbol\n\u001cMeaning\n\u0012\u001cAssociation\n\u001c→\n\u001cSimple link between classes\n\u0012\u001cInheritance (Generalization)\n\u001c🡒 (hollow arrow)\n\u001c\"is-a\" relationship\n\u0012\u001cAggregation\n\u001c◇\n\u001c\"has-a\" weak relationship\n\u0012\u001cComposition\n\u001c◆\n\u001cStrong \"has-a\" (lifetime bound)\n\u0012\u001cDependency\n\u001c──\u003e\n\u001cUses temporarily\n\u0011-\n🔷 Example Class Diagram:\nSystem: Library Management\npgsql\nCopyEdit\n---------------------           --------------------\n|      Book           |         |    Member         |\n|---------------------|         |--------------------|\n| -title: String      |         | -name: String      |\n| -author: String     |         | -id: int           |\n|---------------------|         |--------------------|\n| +getDetails(): void |         | +borrowBook(): void|\n ---------------------           --------------------\n            ↑\n            |\n     ------------------\n    |   TextBook       |\n    |------------------|\n    | -subject: String |\n    -------------------\n\nBook class is inherited by TextBook\u000b\nMember can call borrowBook(), which might use Book.\u000b\n-\n🔷 Kya Use Hai Class Diagram Ka?\n\u0010\u0012\u001cPurpose\n\u001cBenefit\n\u0012\u001cSoftware Design\n\u001cPlanning system architecture\n\u0012\u001cTeam Communication\n\u001cSab developer ek hi design follow karte\n\u0012\u001cObject-Oriented Programming (OOP)\n\u001cOOP structure ko visualize karna\n\u0012\u001cDocumentation\n\u001cFuture reference ke liye helpful\n\u0011-\n🔷 Tools for Drawing Class Diagrams:\nDraw.io (Free)\u000b\nStarUML\u000b\nLucidchart\u000b\nVisual Paradigm\u000b\nEnterprise Architect\u000b\n-\n🔚 Conclusion:\nClass Diagram ek blueprint hota hai object-oriented systems ka. components ko visualize karne ke liye kiya jata hai.\n-\n🔹 UML ki zarurat kyun hai?\nJab aap large ya complex software designing kar rahe hain, tab:\nPure code dekh kar samjhana tough hota hai ki kis Client–Server Architecture\n✅ Kya hota hai?\nA model where client (frontend like browser/mobile) requests something from server (backend like Node.js, Java, etc.), and server gives response.\n✅ Real-life Example:\nClient: Zomato app\u000b\nServer: Zomato backend (menu, orders, payments)\u000b\n✅ Components:\nClient – sends HTTP request (like login, order)\u000b\nServer – processes request and sends back data\u000b\nDatabase – server se connected\u000b\n-\n🔷 2. Database Design (Relational vs NoSQL)\n✅ Relational DB (SQL):\nStructured data, rows and columns\u000b\nFixed schema (tables)\u000b\nExample: MySQL, PostgreSQL\u000b\n✅ NoSQL:\nUnstructured/flexible schema\u000b\nHigh scalability\u000b\nTypes: Document (MongoDB), Key-Value (Redis), Graph (Neo4j)\u000b\n✅ Use-Case:\nSQL for banking, e-commerce\u000b\nNoSQL for chat apps, analytics, dynamic data\u000b\n-\n🔷 3. API Design (REST/GraphQL)\n✅ REST:\nHTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)\u000b\nURL defines resource\u000b\nStateless communication\u000b\n✅ GraphQL:\nSingle endpoint, send query\u000b\nClient decides what fields to fetch\u000b\nOptimized for mobile \u0026 flexible frontends\u000b\n✅ Use-Case:\nREST: Common APIs like login, product APIs\u000b\nGraphQL: Social feeds, dashboards\u000b\n-\n🔷 4. Load Balancer\n✅ Kya karta hai?\nDistributes incoming traffic across multiple servers to:\nAvoid overloading\u000b\nImprove reliability\u000b\n✅ Example:\nAWS ELB, NGINX, HAProxy\u000b\n✅ Use-Case:\nFlipkart website handles 1 lakh users — request evenly distributed to 10 servers.\u000b\n-\n🔷 5. Caching (Redis, Memcached)\n✅ Kya hai?\nTemporary memory storage to quickly fetch frequent data.\n✅ Tools:\nRedis (in-memory + persistent)\u000b\nMemcached (lightweight, volatile)\u000b\n✅ Example:\nStore product catalog in cache to avoid hitting DB again and again.\u000b\n-\n🔷 6. Queue (Kafka, RabbitMQ)\n✅ Kya karta hai?\nQueues asynchronous tasks — like background jobs, logs, notifications.\n✅ Kafka:\nHigh-throughput, distributed log system\u000b\nFor real-time data (streaming)\u000b\n✅ RabbitMQ:\nMessage broker (uses exchange, routing, etc.)\u000b\n✅ Example:\nOrder placed → push to Kafka → background service handles invoice, notification, delivery updates\u000b\n-\n🔷 7. Microservices vs Monolith\n✅ Monolith:\nAll features in one codebase\u000b\nEasy to build, hard to scale\u000b\n✅ Microservices:\nEach feature is an independent service\u000b\nCommunicate via APIs\u000b\n✅ Example:\nZomato:\u000b\nAuth Entity-Relationship (ER) Diagram is a visual representation of how data is structured in a database — it shows:\nEntities (tables)\u000b\nTheir attributes (columns)\u000b\nRelationships between them (foreign keys)\u000b\nYeh diagram mainly database design ke planning phase mein use hota hai, especially before creating actual SQL tables.\n-\n🔧 Example Use-Case: E-commerce System\nSuppose tum ek e-commerce app design kar rahe ho jisme:\nUsers\u000b\nOrders\u000b\nProducts\u000b\nCategories\u000b\nYe sab entities hain — aur unke beech relationships hoti hain.\n-\n🧱 Components of ER Diagram:\n\u0010\u0012\u001cComponent\n\u001cDescription\n\u0012\u001cEntity\n\u001cA real-world object stored in the DB (e.g. User)\n\u0012\u001cAttribute\n\u001cProperties of an entity (e.g. name, email)\n\u0012\u001cPrimary Key\n\u001cUniquely identifies each entity\n\u0012\u001cRelationship\n\u001cLink between two entities\n\u0012\u001cCardinality\n\u001c1:1, 1:N, N:M relations\n\u0011-\n🧩 Basic Example:\nEntities:\nUser\u000b\nOrder\u000b\nAttributes:\nUser → id (PK), name, email\u000b\nOrder → id (PK), order_date, user_id (FK)\u000b\nRelationship:\nA user can place many orders\u000b\nSo it\u0027s a One-to-Many (1:N) relationship\u000b\n-\n✅ ER Diagram:\n[User]\n  ├─ id (PK)\n  ├─ name\n  └─ email\n     │\n     │ 1\n     │──────\u003c places\n     │      N\n[Order]\n  ├─ id (PK)\n  ├─ order_date\n  └─ user_id (FK)\n\n-\n🔢 Cardinality Explained:\n\u0010\u0012\u001cType\n\u001cMeaning\n\u0012\u001c1:1\n\u001cOne user has one profile (rare)\n\u0012\u001c1:N\n\u001cOne user can place many orders\n\u0012\u001cM:N\n\u001cMany students can enroll in many courses\n\u0011-\n🧠 Real-world Example: Student-Course\nEntity 1: Student (id, name)\u000b\nEntity 2: Course (id,              |\n   |           [Enrollment]   |\n   └───────\u003c─── student_id     |\n               course_id ───\u003e─┘\n\nHere, Enrollment is a junction table to manage many-to-many.\n-\n🎯 Why Interview Questions:\n🔸 Q1: What is an ER Diagram?\nAns: A graphical tool used to model entities, attributes, and their relationships in a database.\n🔸 Q2: What is cardinality?\nAns: Defines the Why Normalize?\nImagine ye Caching (Redis, Memcached)\n-\n💡 What is Caching?\nCaching is the process of storing data temporarily in a fast-access memory (usually RAM) so that future requests can be served faster.\n-\n🔍 Real-Life Example:\nTumne Flipkart/Zomato me ek product search kiya → same query dobara ki → result instantly aa gaya?\u000b 🔁 That’s because it came from cache, not database!\n-\n🔧 Why Use Caching?\n\u0010\u0012\u001cNeed\n\u001cSolution with Caching\n\u0012\u001cDB too slow for every request\n\u001cCache the frequently used data\n\u0012\u001cSame data requested again \u0026 again\n\u001cServe from memory (RAM)\n\u0012\u001cReduce server/database load\n\u001cCache reduces repeated hits\n\u0012\u001cImprove user experience\n\u001cPages load much faster\n\u0011-\n🧠 Where Caching is Used:\nscss\nCopyEdit\nClient Request\n    ↓\n[Cache Layer] ← serve if found (fast!)\n    ↓\n[Database] ← fallback if not in cache\n\n-\n🔥 Tools Used for Caching:\n\u0010\u0012\u001cTool\n\u001cType\n\u001cNotes\n\u0012\u001cRedis\n\u001cIn-memory DB\n\u001cVery fast, supports strings, lists\n\u0012\u001cMemcached\n\u001cKey-value store\n\u001cLightweight, simple values only\n\u0012\u001cCDN Cache\n\u001cEdge Cache\n\u001cStatic assets (JS, images, fonts)\n\u0012\u001cBrowser Cache\n\u001cLocal\n\u001cStores CSS, JS for fast reloads\n\u0011-\n🧱 How Caching Works (Flow)\nsql\nCopyEdit\nClient asks: GET /products/123\n\n→ Check in Redis (cache)\n    → If found ✅ → return\n    → If not ❌ → query DB\n        → Save result in Redis\n        → Return to client\n\n-\n⏱️ Cache Expiration (TTL)\nYou can set a TTL (Time To Live) on cache keys, e.g.:\nbash\nCopyEdit\nSET product:123 \"laptop info\" EX 300\n\nThis means: store data for 300 seconds → auto-expire after.\n-\n🔀 Cache Strategies\n\u0010\u0012\u001cStrategy\n\u001cUse Case\n\u0012\u001cRead-through\n\u001cApp reads from cache; if miss, fetch DB\n\u0012\u001cWrite-through\n\u001cApp writes to cache \u0026 DB simultaneously\n\u0012\u001cCache-aside\n\u001cApp manually checks cache → loads → updates\n\u0012\u001cWrite-behind\n\u001cApp
